title: Royal Garden Blues
origin: American jazz-blues standard of 1919 by Clarence Williams and Spencer Williams, named for the Royal Gardens cafe in Chicago; a fixture of the Dixieland and swing repertoire ever since

pd.detail: First published in the United States in 1919; music by Clarence Williams and Spencer Williams. A core Dixieland repertoire number, widely recorded from 1921 onward.
pd.sourceEdition: The standard trad-jazz chart of the composition's final 12-bar riff strain, as common to Dixieland fake-book practice; no single printed edition or recorded arrangement is claimed as the source.
pd.notes: Chart only -- changes and form, no melody and no lyrics. The 1919 publication is multi-strain; only the famous 12-bar blues riff chorus, the strain bands actually jam on, is charted here. The 16-bar verse strains are omitted rather than guessed. The chart is a one-chord-per-bar simplification: each bar carries the chord the bar structurally resolves to (normally beat 1's), so bar 4 is Bb7 (the dominant pull to Eb) and bar 12 is the F7 turnaround; passing chords such as a bar-2 quick change or a bar-9 Cm7 are intentionally flattened. Cut-time readings of the tune map to 4/4 at half the written tempo, which is the grid used here.

notes: The chorus is one of the earliest famous riff strains in jazz: a short riff stated over the I, restated over the IV, answered, then the V7 line home -- a textbook 12-bar blues in Bb. One chord per bar: bar 4 is charted Bb7 (the pull toward Eb), and bar 12 is charted as an F7 turnaround for repeats -- play Bb there on the final pass. Intro and outro are chord-only arrangement vamps, not part of the composition; the outro's Eb-Ebm-Bb is the stock trad-jazz plagal tag. The solo section duplicates the chorus changes so it can be edited independently. Trad performances are a bright two-beat: cut time maps to 4/4 at half the written tempo, so ~104 on this grid is a driving performance tempo.
